Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture
Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Transcendentalism

primary_sources: Noah Webster, An American Dictionary of the English Language, 1828
James Fenimore Cooper, The Last of the Mohicans, 1826
Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, 1845

source: original; documents are public-domain primary sources or paraphrases of them (see each document's sourcing note)
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which a distinct American culture developed in the period 1800-1848.

documents.title: Webster's American dictionary
documents.source: Paraphrase of Noah Webster, An American Dictionary of the English Language, 1828. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A dictionary maker states his purpose: American words spelled the American way.
documents.text: Webster published a dictionary of American English, giving American words American spellings: color for colour, center for centre, defense for defence. He meant the book to belong to the United States, not to Britain, and to teach American children to spell as Americans.

documents.title: Rip Van Winkle wakes up
documents.source: Paraphrase of Washington Irving, "Rip Van Winkle," 1819. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A popular story writer sets a fantasy in an American village after the Revolution.
documents.text: A Dutch settler in the Catskill Mountains falls asleep for twenty years and wakes to a changed village: the portrait of King George III has become one of George Washington, and his neighbors argue about the new republic. The tale mixes humor, fantasy, and a fond look at a simpler past.

documents.title: Cooper's frontier novels
documents.source: Paraphrase of James Fenimore Cooper, The Last of the Mohicans, 1826. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A novelist describes his own frontier stories, which sold widely at home and abroad.
documents.text: Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales follow the frontiersman Natty Bumppo through the forests of New York during the wars of the 1700s. The novels mixed adventure with descriptions of the wilderness and sold widely in the United States and in Europe.

documents.title: Cole paints The Oxbow
documents.source: Thomas Cole, The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm), 1836 (Metropolitan Museum of Art). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A landscape painter shows the American wilderness meeting settled farmland.
documents.text: The painting looks down from a storm-darkened hillside. On the left, a gnarled tree leans over wild forest under black clouds. On the right, the Connecticut River bends through sunny, cleared farmland. A tiny figure with an easel stands on the rocks at lower right.

documents.title: Emerson's American Scholar
documents.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "The American Scholar," address at Cambridge, Massachusetts, August 31, 1837. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A lecturer tells Harvard's Phi Beta Kappa Society that American learning must stand on its own.
documents.text: "Our day of dependence, our long apprenticeship to the learning of other lands, draws to a close. The millions that around us are rushing into life cannot always be fed on the sere remains of foreign harvests. Events, actions arise, that must be sung, that will sing themselves."

documents.title: Emerson on self-reliance
documents.source: Ralph Waldo Emerson, "Self-Reliance," Essays: First Series, 1841. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: An essayist tells readers to trust their own judgment over custom and conformity.
documents.text: "Trust thyself: every heart vibrates to that iron string. Accept the place the divine providence has found for you, the society of your contemporaries, the connection of events."

documents.title: Fuller on women
documents.source: Paraphrase of Margaret Fuller, Woman in the Nineteenth Century, 1845. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A writer in Emerson's circle extends the idea of self-trust to women.
documents.text: Fuller argued that women, like men, should be free to develop their minds and characters. She wrote as a member of the transcendentalist circle in Concord, and her book fed the generation that met for women's rights at Seneca Falls in 1848.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which a distinct American culture developed, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as national pride after the War of 1812, the market revolution, or the expansion of white male democracy.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Hudson River School, Thoreau's Walden, Hawthorne and Melville, or the Lowell Offering.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing where American culture became distinct and where it still borrowed from Europe, or who the new culture included and left out.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: A distinct American culture developed to a great extent between 1800 and 1848, as writers, painters, and thinkers gave American subjects an American voice, yet it stayed rooted in European forms and spoke mostly for white, educated men.
Context: The War of 1812 stirred national pride, the market revolution remade daily life, and white male democracy expanded, all pushing Americans to ask what was American about them.
Grouping: Documents 1, 2, and 3 show the new culture in language and story: Webster's American spellings, Irving's American village tale, and Cooper's frontier novels selling abroad. Documents 4, 5, and 6 show it in paint and philosophy: Cole's wilderness landscape, Emerson's call for intellectual independence, and his doctrine of self-trust. Document 7 extends it: Fuller carries self-trust to women.
Beyond the documents: The Hudson River School painted wilderness where Europe had ruins, Thoreau lived the philosophy at Walden Pond, and Hawthorne and Melville made the Puritan past into American novels.
Complexity: The culture was distinct in subject and voice but European in form — romanticism itself was imported — and its audience was narrow: enslaved people, immigrants, and most women stood outside the circle it celebrated.
